en: The Sūtra on Conditioned Phenomena Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Great Teacher of the Dharma, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Fa Tian, at Nālandā Monastery in Magadha, Central India.
Translated by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!
All conditioned phenomena are subject to change; they are like illusions and lack substantiality, unable to endure for long, devoid of fixed characteristics, and are of a perverted nature."
"O Bhikṣus!
Even all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are exhausted of defilement, unstained, and free from all taints.
All sentient beings, down to the smallest crawling insects and bhūtas, shall certainly perish when their lifespan comes to an end."
If there is no arising for them, then there will likewise be no cessation.

Whether they belong to the caste of householders, brahmins, or kṣatriyas—be they eminent, noble, powerful, or wealthy, possessing immeasurable gold, silver, precious gems, and all manner of enjoyments without lack;
and though they may have parents, kinsmen, relatives, friends, officials, subjects, and servants all fully at their disposal—they cannot escape when their lifespan comes to an end.

Furthermore, once a Kṣatriya has received the consecration, he becomes a great king who attains sovereign power and possesses great might; though his subjects are immeasurable and he brings all lands and territories under his subjection, even he cannot escape when his lifespan comes to its end.
Furthermore, those practitioners in the forest of that seer do not crave flavors and subsist on various fruits;
yet even they, who distance themselves from fruit and practice various austerities, cannot escape when their lifespan comes to an end.

Furthermore, by practicing the ten wholesome paths of action, they are reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

Moreover, by practicing meditative concentration, they attain the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, and the Mahābrahmā Heaven; the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, and the Ābhāsvara Heaven; the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, and the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; and the Anabhraka Heaven, the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, and the Asaṃjñisattva Heaven.
Furthermore, those who are non-returners (anāgāmin) attain the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

Furthermore, those who, weary of and repelled by the physical body, cultivate the samādhis of infinite space and so forth, attain birth in the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception;
although these various devas are preeminent, they are not exempt from being born there, nor do they escape death and destruction.

"If they have exhausted the outflows of the three realms, accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, destroyed all fetters of existence, and realized arhatship— though this body of theirs must also eventually be cast aside;
or if, during the kalpa of weapons, they cultivate themselves alone in solitude, awaken to all causes and conditions, and attain the realization of the Middle Vehicle, being called pratyekabuddhas—
though this body of theirs must also eventually be cast aside."

Even the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—possessing the vastness of the ten powers, the perfect clarity of the four knowledges, fearlessness in preaching the Dharma, and the true lion’s roar—who attained the Nārāyaṇa body through countless hardships, likewise relinquished it.
“O Bhikṣus! It is like those potters who fashion earthenware vessels such as basins and jars; though they are successfully completed, they are certain to break.
Or again, it is like fruit that, once ripe, must naturally fall. Such is the nature of arising and ceasing.”
"O Bhikṣus!
All sentient beings, even down to the *bhūtas*, all conscious creatures until the end of their lifespan—none can escape this.
As there is no such thing as birth, so too shall there be no death."
He further spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata, the God among Gods, Has taught this dharma of impermanence:
Like an unbaked earthen vessel that is not firm, It ultimately tends toward destruction.”
"Just as fruit ripens and falls of its own accord, so too is the life of sentient beings.
Bhikṣus, you should know this now: one ought to feel dread toward birth and death.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished speaking this sutra, the assembly of bhikṣus received it with single-minded faith and joyfully put it into practice.
The Sūtra on All Conditioned Phenomena Spoken by the Buddha
